why_how.text: Your license is a privilege, and your driving record is how the state tracks whether you keep earning it.
Convictions from any state land on your Michigan record, and some stay for years or for good.
Extenuating circumstances belong in court, because the Secretary of State cannot set aside a court conviction.

scenario.text: Dana gets a speeding ticket on a trip through another state and decides to ignore it because she is home now.

reasoning.text: Crashes and convictions from other states are reported to Michigan, and ignoring a ticket usually leads to license suspension.

result.text: Dana answers the ticket; the conviction can still appear on her Michigan record with Michigan points.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a ticket from another state never reaches your Michigan record.

correction.text: Other states report crashes and convictions to Michigan, and they appear on your record with points under the Michigan system.

prompt.text: A driver wants to explain to the Secretary of State why her ticket was unfair after the court convicted her. Will that work?

answer.text: No. Extenuating circumstances must be raised in court.

rationale.text: The Secretary of State cannot set aside a court conviction, so the court is the place to explain.

lines.text: Your record tracks how you drive.

narration.text: This lesson is about your driving record. In Michigan, a license is a privilege you keep only by continuing to show safe driving skill and knowledge. If you do not, the license may be restricted, suspended or revoked. Your record is the history the state uses to make those decisions. We will look at what goes on the record, who reports it, how long it stays, who can see it, and what happens when tickets are ignored or argued in the wrong place. Each of these rules shows up in practice questions, and each one also matters in real life when a ticket arrives.

lines.text: A license is kept through safe driving.
Police and courts report to the state.
Some drug crimes are listed too.

narration.text: Start with the idea of privilege. A license is a privilege you keep only by continuing to show safe driving skill and knowledge, or it may be restricted, suspended or revoked. The record is how that showing is measured. Your record lists civil or criminal moving violations and crashes. Those are reported to the Secretary of State by police and courts, along with certain drug crimes. So you do not report your own tickets. The officers and courts who handle them do. When a question asks who reports a conviction, the answer is police and courts, not you and not your insurer.

lines.text: Most stay at least seven years.
Some ten; fatal or impaired, forever.

narration.text: Your record follows you across state lines. Crashes and convictions from other states are reported to Michigan and appear on your record, with points assessed under the Michigan system. So a ticket on a road trip counts at home. Next, how long things stay. Most convictions stay on your record for at least seven years. Some convictions and licensing actions stay for at least ten years. A fatality or an impaired driving conviction stays permanently. Keep the three lengths in order: seven for most, ten for some, and forever for the most serious ones. Questions often swap these.

lines.text: Only permissible uses set by law.

narration.text: Your record is not open to anyone who asks. The Driver Privacy Protection Act keeps personal record details private, except for permissible uses set by law. Examples of those uses are insurance rating, vehicle recalls, and rental car driver checks. So an insurer may use your record to rate your policy, and a carmaker may use it to reach you about a recall, but a stranger cannot simply look it up. This matters because the record holds a lot about you. The law balances privacy against a short list of uses that serve drivers and safety. Remember the pattern: private, with listed exceptions.

lines.text: Ignoring a ticket leads to suspension.

narration.text: Traffic violations may be civil infractions, misdemeanors or felonies. Whatever the type, ignoring a ticket usually leads to license suspension. Getting more tickets while suspended makes it worse. Moving violation tickets received while suspended bring more suspensions and a reinstatement fee. Finally, if you think there were extenuating circumstances, you must raise them in court. The Secretary of State cannot set aside a court conviction. So the order is simple: answer the ticket, explain yourself to the court if you need to, and never drive on a suspended license. Each step protects your record from growing.

lines.text: Trap: the conviction leaves with the points.
Convictions stay seven years or longer.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Points and convictions run on different clocks. Points stay on the record for two years from the conviction date. The conviction itself stays much longer: at least seven years for most, at least ten for some, and permanently for a fatality or impaired driving conviction. Options may say a conviction disappears when its points do, or that an impaired driving conviction drops off after seven years. Both are wrong. When a question asks how long something stays, first decide whether it is asking about points or about the conviction. Then pick the matching length.

Here is a quick check: a driver was convicted in court on a ticket she thinks was unfair. She plans to explain the circumstances to the Secretary of State afterward. Will that work? Recall who can undo a conviction. The Secretary of State cannot set aside a court conviction. That is why extenuating circumstances must be raised in court, before or at the time the case is decided. So the answer is no. Her chance to explain was in court. The lesson for any driver is to treat the court date as the moment that counts, and not to expect a later office visit to change it.

To finish, a license is a privilege you keep by showing safe driving skill and knowledge. Police and courts report moving violations, crashes and certain drug crimes to the Secretary of State, and other states report their convictions to Michigan with Michigan points. Most convictions stay at least seven years, some at least ten, and fatal or impaired driving convictions stay forever. Record details stay private except for permissible uses. Ignoring a ticket usually means suspension, tickets while suspended add more, and circumstances belong in court. The hook is seven, ten, or forever.

why_how.text: Points measure recent risk, so they post only after a conviction and fade after two years.
Too many points or one-point violations in two years trigger a driver assessment reexamination.

scenario.text: Marcus has seven one-point violations over the last two years, but only seven points in total.

reasoning.text: Six or more one-point violations within two years require a reexamination, even when the total is under twelve.

result.text: Marcus will face a driver assessment reexamination.

claim.text: Myth: your state record points are the same points your insurer uses.

correction.text: State record points are separate from the points an insurance company uses to set your rate.

prompt.text: A driver has collected twelve points within the last two years. What follows?

rationale.text: Twelve or more points within two years require the reexamination, just as six one-point violations do.

narration.text: This lesson explains how points work on your Michigan driving record. Points are the state's way of tracking recent risky driving. Their values are set in the Michigan Vehicle Code. We will cover when points are posted, how long they stay, what totals send you to a driver assessment reexamination, and why your state points are not the same as the points your insurance company uses. These rules connect to each other, so it helps to learn them as one system. Practice questions often test the time window and the thresholds, so we will keep those numbers clear and side by side.

lines.text: Values set in the Vehicle Code.

narration.text: Points are posted only after a moving violation conviction. A ticket by itself does not post points. The conviction does. The values for each violation are set in the Michigan Vehicle Code. Once posted, points stay on the record for two years from the conviction date. After that they drop off. But remember the other clock. The convictions behind those points stay on the record much longer: at least seven years for most, at least ten for some, and permanently for fatal or impaired driving convictions. So when the points are gone, the history is still there for anyone with a permissible use.

There are two ways points can send you to a driver assessment reexamination. The first is six or more one-point violations within a two-year period. The second is twelve or more points within a two-year period. Either one is enough. Both are measured within two years, which matches how long points stay. So a driver with many small violations can be called in even if the total never reaches twelve, and a driver with a few serious violations can be called in by reaching twelve. Keep the pair together: six small ones, or twelve points, in two years.

lines.text: State points sit on your record.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people think the points on their state driving record are the same points their insurance company uses. They are not. State record points are separate from the points an insurance company uses to set your rate. So an option claiming that clearing state points automatically lowers insurance points, or that insurers simply copy the state total, is wrong. Your state record points decide things like reexaminations. Your insurer runs its own system for pricing. When a question mixes the two, pick the answer that keeps them apart.

Here is a quick check: a driver has collected twelve points within the last two years. What follows? Recall the two thresholds. Six or more one-point violations within two years require a driver assessment reexamination, and so do twelve or more points within two years. This driver has reached twelve points inside the window. So the answer is a driver assessment reexamination. If the same twelve points had been spread over a longer time, some would have dropped off after two years, and the total inside the window would be lower. The window is what makes the count.

To finish, points are posted only after a moving violation conviction, with values set in the Michigan Vehicle Code, and they stay on the record for two years from the conviction date. The convictions behind them stay much longer. Six or more one-point violations, or twelve or more points, within two years require a driver assessment reexamination. And your state record points are separate from the points an insurance company uses to set your rate. The hook to keep is two years for points, and the pair to keep is six small violations or twelve points within that window.

why_how.text: Points rise with danger, so the most harmful acts carry six points and minor moving violations carry two.
Speeding points step up by band, so how far over the limit you were decides the points.
Refusals differ by test: a chemical alcohol test refusal is six points, an underage Preliminary Breath Test refusal is two.

scenario.text: Lee is convicted of driving fourteen miles per hour over the limit.

reasoning.text: Eleven to fifteen miles per hour over the limit is a three-point violation; sixteen or more over would be four.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating every alcohol-related violation as worth the same points.

correction.text: Operating while intoxicated is six points, impaired driving and any bodily alcohol under twenty-one are four, and an open container is two.

prompt.text: A nineteen-year-old driver refuses a Preliminary Breath Test. How many points is that?

rationale.text: A Preliminary Breath Test refusal under twenty-one is two points, while refusing a chemical alcohol test is six.

narration.text: This lesson sorts violations by the points they carry. Michigan uses four main levels: six points, four points, three points and two points. The more dangerous the act, the higher the level. We will walk through each level, then look at the pairs that people confuse most: speeding bands, test refusals, intoxicated versus impaired driving, and the two kinds of failure to yield. Practice questions usually name one violation and ask for its points, or name a point value and ask which violation fits. Learning the levels as groups makes both kinds of question easier to answer.

Six points is the top level. Six-point violations include manslaughter, negligent homicide or another vehicle felony, operating while intoxicated or with any Schedule one drug or cocaine, and failing to stop and identify yourself at a crash. Also at six points are reckless driving, refusing a chemical alcohol test, fleeing or eluding police, and any moving violation causing injury or death. One more belongs here: a failure to yield that causes death or injury to an emergency responder, a construction worker, or a person operating animal husbandry implements. The common thread is serious harm or serious defiance of the law.

Four-point violations are drag racing, impaired driving, any bodily alcohol content under age twenty-one, and going sixteen miles per hour or more over the limit. Three-point violations are careless driving, disobeying a signal or stop sign, improper passing, eleven to fifteen miles per hour over the limit, not stopping at a railroad crossing, and not stopping for a school bus or crossing guard. Notice that the three-point list is about ignoring controls and other road users, while the four-point list adds alcohol and racing. Both lists carry a speeding band, which we will compare in a moment.

lines.text: Six to ten over the limit.

narration.text: Two points is the base level. Two-point violations are six to ten miles per hour over the limit, an open alcohol container, a Preliminary Breath Test refusal under twenty-one, failing to yield or use caution for emergency vehicles, and all other moving violations. That last part matters: if a moving violation is not named on a higher list, it is a two-point violation. Failing to yield shows how harm moves a violation up. Simply failing to yield to emergency vehicles costs two points, but a failure to yield that kills or injures an emergency responder costs six. No harm points to two; harm points to six.

lines.text: Six to ten over: two points.

narration.text: Speeding points step up by band. Six to ten miles per hour over the limit earns two points. Eleven to fifteen miles per hour over earns three. Sixteen miles per hour or more over earns four. So the question is always how far over the limit you were. A driver at thirteen over is in the middle band and gets three. A driver at sixteen over has crossed into the top band and gets four. A driver at eight over is in the lowest band and gets two. Draw the three bands in your mind like steps, and place the speed on the right step before choosing the points.

Here is the trap. Two kinds of test refusal carry very different points. Refusing a chemical alcohol test carries six points, while a driver under twenty-one refusing a Preliminary Breath Test gets two. Alcohol levels split the same way. Operating while intoxicated is a six-point violation, while impaired driving and any bodily alcohol under twenty-one are four-point violations. An option that gives impaired driving six points, or gives every refusal six, is wrong. Read the exact words in the question: chemical test or breath test, intoxicated or impaired. Those words decide the points.

Here is a quick check: a nineteen-year-old driver refuses a Preliminary Breath Test. How many points is that? Recall the two refusals. Refusing a chemical alcohol test is a six-point violation. A Preliminary Breath Test refusal under twenty-one is on the two-point list. This driver is under twenty-one and refused the Preliminary Breath Test, not the chemical test. So the answer is two points. If the same driver had refused a chemical alcohol test, the answer would be six. The test named in the question, and the driver's age, are what decide which list applies.

To finish, six-point violations include vehicle felonies, operating while intoxicated, leaving a crash without identifying yourself, reckless driving, refusing a chemical alcohol test, fleeing police, and failures to yield that hurt a responder or worker. Four points covers drag racing, impaired driving, any bodily alcohol under twenty-one and sixteen or more over. Three points covers careless driving, signals, improper passing, eleven to fifteen over, railroad crossings and school buses. Everything else, including six to ten over and an open container, is two. The hook is six, four, three, two.

why_how.text: Every standard drink holds about the same alcohol, so the type of drink does not change its effect.
Even one drink slows reaction and dulls attention, so the only safe plan is not driving after drinking.
Never let an impaired person drive or ride with one; take their keys if needed and offer a place to sleep.

scenario.text: After two beers, Sam drinks coffee and walks outside before deciding to drive home.

reasoning.text: Coffee, cold showers, exercise and fresh air do not sober you up; only time does.

result.text: Sam is not sober; he should use a sober driver, a ride, a taxi or public transportation.

claim.text: Myth: beer is weaker than wine or whiskey, so it affects you less.

correction.text: Beer, wine and whiskey affect you the same way, because standard servings can hold the same amount of alcohol.

prompt.text: Your friend has been drinking and reaches for the car keys. What should you do?

answer.text: Do not let your friend drive; take the keys if needed and offer a place to sleep.

rationale.text: Never let an impaired person drive or ride with one, and take their keys if needed.

narration.text: This lesson is about alcohol and driving. We will look at why beer, wine and whiskey affect you the same way, what even one drink does to your driving, why common sobering tricks fail, and how to plan so that no one drives impaired. These ideas are short, but they carry a lot of weight, because they change real choices at the end of an evening. Practice questions in this area usually test a myth, such as coffee sobering you up, or ask for the safest plan. If you keep the three ideas at the top of the slide in mind, most of those questions answer themselves.

lines.text: Shot, glass of wine, can of beer.
Each can hold the same alcohol.

narration.text: Beer, wine and whiskey affect you the same way. The reason is the serving size. A one point five-ounce whiskey shot, a five-ounce wine glass and a twelve-ounce beer can each hold the same amount of alcohol. So switching from liquor to beer does not make you safer. What matters is how many standard drinks you have had. And any standard drink affects your judgment and self-control. That is important because judgment is what you use to decide whether you are fit to drive. Alcohol weakens the very skill you would need to notice that you are impaired.

Even one drink can impair driving. It does this in three ways. It slows your reaction time, so you take longer to brake or steer when something happens. It dulls your concentration, so you notice hazards later. And it can cause vision problems. Each of these alone raises the risk of a crash, and together they add up quickly. This is why waiting until you feel drunk is not a safe test. Impairment starts before you feel it. The safest way to think about it is simple: if you have had a drink, your driving is already affected, even if you feel fine.

lines.text: Pick a sober driver in advance.
Or use a ride, taxi or transit.

narration.text: The best plan is never to drink and drive. That means making the decision before the first drink, not after. Choose a sober designated driver in advance, or get a ride, a taxi or public transportation. Planning ahead matters because alcohol affects judgment, so a decision made later is made by an impaired mind. You also have a role when others drink. Never let an impaired person drive, and never ride with one. Take their keys if needed and offer a place to sleep. These steps are simple, and they work best when everyone knows the plan from the start.

lines.text: Trap: coffee or a cold shower sobers.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Coffee, a cold shower, exercise or fresh air may feel sobering, but time is the only thing that removes alcohol's effects. Coffee can make you feel more awake, and cold air can make you feel alert, but your reaction time and judgment are still impaired. Options on a practice question may offer any of these as a way to sober up. All of them are wrong. The only correct answer is time. This trap is dangerous because feeling better is easy to mistake for being better. If you have been drinking, a cup of coffee does not make you a safe driver.

Here is a quick check: your friend has been drinking and reaches for the car keys to drive home. What should you do? Recall the rule for other people. Never let an impaired person drive or ride with one. Take their keys if needed and offer a place to sleep. So the answer is to stop your friend from driving and give them a safe option, such as staying over. Riding along to keep them awake, or following behind in your own car, does not make the trip safe. A short trip is still a trip with an impaired driver at the wheel, and it puts everyone on the road at risk.

To finish, beer, wine and whiskey affect you the same way, because a standard shot, glass of wine and beer can each hold the same amount of alcohol. Any standard drink affects judgment and self-control, and even one drink can slow reaction time, dull concentration and cause vision problems. Coffee, cold showers, exercise and fresh air do not sober you up; only time does. The best plan is never to drink and drive, with a sober designated driver chosen in advance, and never letting an impaired person drive or ride with one. The hook is only time sobers.

why_how.text: Drug convictions suspend a license even when no driving was involved, because the law ties the license to the conviction itself.
Repeat drug offenses within seven years bring longer suspensions and longer waits for a restricted license.

scenario.text: Riley, with no prior drug violations, is convicted of drug possession that had nothing to do with driving.

reasoning.text: Drug convictions require suspension even if you were not driving; with no priors it lasts six months, with no restricted license for thirty days.

result.text: Riley's license is suspended for six months, and no restricted license is issued for the first thirty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a drug conviction only affects your license if you were caught driving.

correction.text: Drug convictions require license suspension even if you were not driving, and possession, manufacture or distribution alone can trigger it.

memory_support.text: Six and thirty, one year and sixty.

prompt.text: A driver with a drug conviction five years ago is convicted again. How long is the suspension, and when could a restricted license come?

answer.text: One year, with no restricted license for the first sixty days.

rationale.text: A prior drug conviction within seven years means a one-year suspension with no restricted license for sixty days.

narration.text: This lesson covers how drug convictions affect your license. The key idea surprises many people: a drug conviction can suspend your license even when no car was involved. We will look at what triggers the suspension, how long it lasts for a first offense and for a repeat, when a restricted license may be issued, and the separate reinstatement fee. Practice questions here often test the two suspension lengths side by side, so we will keep the first offense and the repeat offense clearly apart, with the matching waiting period for each, and end with the fee that applies.

lines.text: Suspension even if you were not driving.

narration.text: Drug convictions require license suspension even if you were not driving. Possession, manufacture or distribution alone can trigger it. So the suspension follows the conviction, not the vehicle. A person arrested at home, with no car anywhere nearby, can still lose driving privileges after a drug conviction. This is different from most of the violations in the points lessons, which happen behind the wheel. Here the license is affected by a crime that may have nothing to do with driving at all. When a question asks whether driving was needed for the suspension, the answer is no.

lines.text: No restricted license for thirty days.
Repeat in seven years: one year, sixty days.

narration.text: With no prior drug violations, the suspension lasts six months, and no restricted license is issued for the first thirty days. With one or more prior drug convictions within seven years, the suspension is one year, with no restricted license for the first sixty days. So both the suspension and the waiting period double for a repeat. Six months becomes one year, and thirty days becomes sixty. The seven-year window is what makes an earlier conviction count as a prior. Keep the pairs together: six months and thirty days for a first offense, one year and sixty days for a repeat.

Here is the trap. A first drug offense means a six-month suspension with no restricted license for thirty days, while a repeat within seven years means one year with none for sixty days. Options often mix the parts, such as six months with sixty days, or one year with thirty days. Others reverse them entirely. All of those are wrong. Another trap is treating the thirty days as the whole suspension. Thirty days is only the period with no restricted license, inside a six-month suspension. Read whether the question asks about the suspension length or about the restricted license wait.

lines.text: Prior drug conviction five years ago.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver had a drug conviction five years ago and is now convicted again. How long is the suspension, and when could a restricted license come? Recall the seven-year window. One or more prior drug convictions within seven years means a one-year suspension with no restricted license for the first sixty days. Five years is inside the window, so the earlier conviction counts. The answer is one year, with no restricted license for sixty days. If this were the driver's first drug conviction, the answer would be six months with thirty days instead.

lines.text: Six and thirty; one year and sixty.

narration.text: To finish, drug convictions require license suspension even if you were not driving, and possession, manufacture or distribution alone can trigger it. With no prior drug violations the suspension lasts six months, with no restricted license for the first thirty days. A prior drug conviction within seven years means one year, with none for the first sixty days. The drug suspension reinstatement fee is one hundred twenty-five dollars, separate from any other reinstatement fee. The hook is six and thirty, one year and sixty, and the fee is its own charge on top of any others.

why_how.text: Marijuana distorts your sense of time, space and speed, so driving impaired by it is illegal even where using it is legal.
By applying for or renewing a license you agree to chemical testing, so refusing brings a suspension.

scenario.text: Taylor, age twenty-five, legally carries marijuana in the car and smokes some before driving home.

reasoning.text: Transport within the limit is legal, but operating a vehicle under its influence, or consuming it while doing so, is illegal.

result.text: Taylor faces the same penalties as a drunk driver, including up to ninety-three days in jail and six points.

claim.text: Myth: if marijuana is legal for you to carry, driving after using it is legal too.

correction.text: Carrying up to two point five ounces is legal for adults twenty-one or older, yet driving under its influence carries the same penalties as drunk driving.

memory_support.text: Legal to carry, illegal to drive.

prompt.text: An officer asks a driver for a chemical test after field sobriety tests. The driver says he never agreed to testing. Is he right?

answer.text: No. He agreed by applying for or renewing his license.

rationale.text: Under implied consent, every driver agrees to chemical testing by applying for or renewing a license, and refusing brings a suspension.

lines.text: Legal to carry is not legal to drive.

narration.text: This lesson covers marijuana and chemical testing. Marijuana is legal for adults in Michigan, but legal use and safe driving are two different things. We will look at what adults may transport, what is illegal while operating a vehicle, how officers judge impairment, what the implied consent law means, and what penalties apply to driving under the influence. The thread through the whole lesson is a single contrast: what you may carry is one rule, and how you may drive is another. Practice questions like to blur that contrast, so we will keep the two sides clearly apart throughout.

lines.text: Up to two point five ounces.
No more than fifteen grams concentrate.

narration.text: Adults twenty-one or older may legally transport up to two point five ounces of marijuana, with no more than fifteen grams as concentrate. That is the carrying rule. But even where marijuana is legal, driving while impaired by it is illegal and unsafe, because it distorts your sense of time, space and speed. Those are exactly the senses you use to judge gaps, follow at a safe distance and choose a safe speed. So the transport limit tells you what may be in the car. It says nothing about using marijuana and then driving. Keep that line clear before moving on to the operating rules.

lines.text: No smoking in the passenger area.

narration.text: It is illegal to operate or be in physical control of a motor vehicle, aircraft, snowmobile, off-road vehicle or motorboat while under the influence of marijuana, or to consume it while doing so. Notice how wide the list is. It is not only cars. Notice also physical control, which covers more than actively driving. In addition, drivers and passengers may not smoke marijuana in a vehicle's passenger area on a public way. So a passenger lighting up is breaking the law too. And taking marijuana into Canada is illegal, even though Michigan allows adult possession at home.

Officers judge impairment from your driving, their observations, and standardized and non-standardized field sobriety tests, and they may request a chemical test. Under the implied consent law, every driver agrees to chemical testing by applying for or renewing a license. Refusing the test brings a license suspension. So the agreement is made long before any traffic stop. It comes with the license itself. And refusing a chemical alcohol test is a six-point violation, as you saw in the points lesson. That makes refusal costly in two ways: the suspension and the points on your record.

title.text: Legal to carry, not to drive

narration.text: Here is the trap. Carrying up to two point five ounces of marijuana is legal for adults twenty-one or older, yet driving under its influence carries the same penalties as drunk driving. Those penalties include up to ninety-three days in jail, up to a five hundred dollars fine, suspension and six points, with tougher penalties when minors are in the vehicle. Options may suggest that legal possession lowers the penalty, or that marijuana impairment is only a minor ticket. Both are wrong. The penalties match alcohol. Possession rules and driving rules are separate, and the driving rule is strict.

Here is a quick check: after field sobriety tests, an officer asks a driver for a chemical test. The driver says he never agreed to any testing. Is he right? Recall the implied consent law. Every driver agrees to chemical testing by applying for or renewing a license. So the driver did agree, at the moment he applied for or renewed his license, even if he does not remember it. The answer is no. If he refuses, the refusal brings a license suspension. Officers may request this test after judging impairment from driving, observations and field sobriety tests.

lines.text: Legal to carry, illegal to drive.

narration.text: To finish, adults twenty-one or older may transport up to two point five ounces of marijuana, with no more than fifteen grams as concentrate, but driving while impaired by it is illegal and unsafe because it distorts time, space and speed. Operating a car, boat, snowmobile, off-road vehicle or aircraft under its influence is illegal, and no one may smoke it in a vehicle's passenger area on a public way. Officers judge impairment and may request a chemical test, which every licensed driver has agreed to. The penalties match alcohol. The hook is legal to carry, illegal to drive.

why_how.text: A reexamination lets the state check that a driver is still safe after health concerns, crashes or a poor record.
New drivers are held to a tighter standard, so one or two violations can bring a reexamination.

scenario.text: Jordan, a GDL driver, gets two tickets in a few months, while her uncle has two tickets and no crashes.

reasoning.text: Probationary and GDL drivers may face reexamination after one or two violations; ordinary drivers face it at twelve points or three crashes in two years.

result.text: Jordan may be called in for a reexamination; her uncle has not reached the ordinary-driver triggers.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a reexamination always ends with a revoked license.

correction.text: A reexamination reviews your driving and sets controls such as restrictions, suspensions, revocations or a mix, and you are told your appeal rights.

memory_support.text: Twelve, three, or one or two.

prompt.text: A driver has had three property-damage crashes in the last two years and no tickets. Can the state call her in for a reexamination?

answer.text: Yes. Three or more crashes in two years allow a reexamination.

rationale.text: Three or more injury or property-damage crashes in two years, or twelve or more points in two years, allow a reexamination.

lines.text: A review, not an automatic penalty.

narration.text: This lesson covers reexaminations. The Secretary of State may reexamine you for health concerns, violating license restrictions, crash involvement or a poor driving record. A reexamination is a review of whether you are still safe to drive. We will look at the legal grounds, the crash and point thresholds, the tighter standard for new drivers, what happens during the review, and what a medical reexamination may require. Practice questions often compare ordinary drivers with probationary and GDL drivers, so we will keep those two groups side by side, along with the numbers that trigger a call-in for each group.

lines.text: Unsafe physical, visual or mental condition.
Fatal crash showing negligence or drinking.

narration.text: Several legal grounds allow a reexamination. One is unfitness, or an unsafe physical, visual or mental condition. Another is a fatal crash where the report shows negligence or drinking. A third is a conviction for violating license restrictions. These grounds share one idea: something suggests the driver may not be safe, so the state takes a closer look. They are not about paperwork mistakes or ordinary life changes. Moving house or buying a car does not trigger a review. A condition, a serious crash, or ignoring the limits already placed on your license does, and any one of them is enough.

lines.text: Three or more crashes in two years.

narration.text: A driving record can also trigger a reexamination. Three or more injury or property-damage crashes in two years allow a reexamination. So do twelve or more points in two years. Notice that both are measured within two years, the same window that points use. A driver does not need any tickets to be called in. Three crashes are enough on their own. And a driver does not need any crashes. Twelve points are enough on their own. These are the triggers for ordinary drivers. As the next slide shows, new drivers can be called in much sooner, after far fewer violations.

lines.text: One or two violations may do it.

narration.text: Probationary and GDL drivers may face a reexamination after just one or two violations. That is a much tighter standard than for ordinary drivers. The reason is that new drivers are still building skill, so early warning signs get attention right away. Compare the two groups. Ordinary drivers face reexamination at twelve points or three crashes in two years. Probationary and GDL drivers may be called in after one or two violations. So a teen driver with two tickets may be reviewed, while an experienced driver with the same two tickets has not reached the ordinary triggers. The gap is large.

lines.text: Reviews your driving with an analyst.
You learn appeal and reinstatement steps.

narration.text: A reexamination reviews your driving and sets licensing controls, such as restrictions, suspensions, revocations or a mix of them. A driver analyst reviews your record with you. If your license is restricted, suspended or revoked, you are told your appeal rights and reinstatement steps. So the outcome is not fixed in advance. It depends on the review. A medical reexamination may require vision, written and on-road tests, and current medical, vision or psychological information. That lets the state match the controls to the actual concern instead of applying one penalty to everyone.

lines.text: Trap: one rule for every driver.
Ordinary: twelve points or three crashes.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Ordinary drivers face reexamination at twelve points or three crashes in two years, while probationary and GDL drivers may be called in after one or two violations. Options may give new drivers the twelve-point line, or claim that GDL drivers get more leeway because they are still learning. Both are wrong. New drivers are held to the tighter standard. Another trap is reversing the groups, giving ordinary drivers the one-or-two rule. When a question names a probationary or GDL driver, think one or two. When it names any other driver, think twelve points or three crashes.

Here is a quick check: a driver has had three property-damage crashes in the last two years and no tickets at all. Can the state call her in for a reexamination? Recall the record triggers. Three or more injury or property-damage crashes in two years allow a reexamination, and so do twelve or more points in two years. Either trigger works on its own. She has three crashes inside the window, so the answer is yes, even with no points. Her reexamination would then review her driving and could set restrictions or other controls, and she would be told her rights.

lines.text: Twelve, three, or one or two.

narration.text: To finish, the Secretary of State may reexamine you for health concerns, violating restrictions, crash involvement or a poor record. Legal grounds include unsafe conditions, fatal crashes showing negligence or drinking, and restriction violations. Three or more crashes or twelve or more points in two years allow a reexamination, while probationary and GDL drivers may be called in after one or two violations. A driver analyst reviews your record, may set controls, and explains appeal rights and reinstatement steps. For new drivers and parents, Michigan.gov slash NewDrivers collects driver education, GDL, parent coaching and teen risk resources.
